analysis.one_liner: Cuts the federal trigger level for lead in drinking water from 15 to 5 parts per billion.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee with no cosponsors and never received a hearing or vote before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After lead contaminated Flint, Michigan's water, this bill would have required the EPA to tighten the 'action level' for lead in drinking water — the contamination threshold that forces public water systems to take action, such as controlling pipe corrosion. It set a deadline of 10 parts per billion by the end of 2020 and 5 parts per billion by the end of 2026, down from the current 15. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never went anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Families served by water systems with lead pipes or lead solder, especially children, whose developing brains are most harmed by lead exposure. Lowering the action level means more water systems would be required to control corrosion — the main way lead gets from old pipes into tap water.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families drinking water from lead pipes

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA to revise the lead drinking water rule so the action level falls to no more than 10 parts per billion by the end of 2020 and 5 parts per billion by the end of 2026, from the current 15 parts per billion [S2][S3].
An action level is the contamination threshold that triggers additional required actions by a public water system, such as controlling the corrosion that leaches lead from pipes into tap water [S2].
Lowering that threshold means more water systems nationwide would be legally required to take protective action against lead reaching customers' taps [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Public water systems, which would have to do more corrosion control and related treatment to meet the lower threshold; those costs can be passed on to water customers. Communities with older lead infrastructure would face the largest bills.

drawbacks.text: Lowering the action level from 15 to 10 and then 5 parts per billion would require many water systems to add or intensify corrosion-control treatment, a real cost that would fall partly on water customers, with the heaviest burden on systems serving older communities [S2][S3].
The bill set deadlines in statute but provided no dedicated funding for water systems to meet them, leaving compliance costs to be covered by local ratepayers or future appropriations [S3].

The bill addressed only the trigger threshold for lead in drinking water; it did not fund replacement of lead service lines, so systems could face pressure to treat symptoms of aging lead pipes rather than remove them [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — less lead in children's drinking water — is a genuine public health gain, since no level of lead exposure is considered safe. The cost is real but ordinary for environmental regulation: water systems would need to invest in corrosion control, and ratepayers would bear some of it. A fairer design would have paired the stricter standard with federal money to help small and older systems comply.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which referred it to a subcommittee, and it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2017 — no hearing, no vote, no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Rep. Dan Kildee, whose district includes Flint, Michigan, introduced the bill on April 28, 2016 [S1][S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced [S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Environment and the Economy, where it stayed; no further action was taken for the rest of the Congress [S5].
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Water systems avoided a stricter, costlier lead-control requirement, and the committee system kept a bill with zero cosponsors from reaching the floor. Families exposed to lead in drinking water got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Water utilities; families got no protection

for.name: Rep. Dan Kildee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to lower the lead action level in drinking water; it was his only action before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Environment and the Economy and never reported it out, held no hearing, and never scheduled it for a vote.

against.name: Subcommittee on Environment and the Economy
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 29, 2016 and took no action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, and it died in a committee controlled by Republicans without ever reaching the floor [S4][S5].

industries.note: A lower action level would have forced more systems to install or intensify corrosion control and other lead-mitigation steps, with compliance costs passed to ratepayers. Utilities that dodged the 15 parts per billion trigger would have been pulled under a tighter one.
